newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Taiwan questions HK future, business splashes out.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan questions HK future, business splashes out.

text.p: Taiwan on Tuesday voiced doubts about Hong Kong's future under Chinese rule as the territory's capitalists unveiled a multi-million dollar extravaganza to mark the handover from Britain.

With a third batch of 90 People's Liberation Army soldiers on the way, the territory's future leader Tung Chee-hwa, responding to public pressure, invited submissions on a plan to change election rules after Hong Kong reverts to Beijing in 35 days at midnight on June 30.
Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui hailed Hong Kong's return to China after more than 150 years as a British colony, but questioned Hong Kong's chances of flourishing under Beijing's control.
"From the Chinese point of view, Hong Kong's transfer to mainland China is a delightful thing," said Lee, whose exiled Republic of China regards Hong Kong as part of China.

"But as for its transfer to the communist system, I am concerned whether Hong Kong can maintain a high degree of growth in its future development. Its prospects are both suspicious and worrisome," he said.

But Hong Kong's business community will splash out on the return to China with a HK$100 million (US$12.8 million) show of fireworks, lasers, an illuminated barge flotilla and giant balloons marking the first day of Chinese rule on July 1.
More than 30 big business have lined up to sponsor the event, organised by the Better Hong Kong Foundation which is an affiliation of Hong Kong's billionaire businessmen.

The sponsors include key representatives of the British colonial establishment, Jardine Matheson Holdings Ltd and John Swire & Sons (Hong Kong) Ltd, names synonomous with the colonial rule of Hong Kong.
The one-hour show will feature what the organisers bill as the world's largest outdoor karaoke show.

The colonial government announced on Tuesday China would send more PLA soldiers to Hong Kong on Friday to prepare for the takeover from withdrawing British troops. Beijing already has sent 106 soldiers to territory.
Tung's office said in a statement it had invited the public to submit views on China-inspired changes to Hong Kong election laws.

Governor Chris Patten and the pro-democracy movement in Hong Kong have criticised the plan to change the current electoral rules for the 60-seat legislature as a ploy that would slash the number of democrats who could be elected.

The leader of Hong Kong's popular Democratic Party, Martin Lee, said he would press Britain to defend the territory's currently elected legislature during talks with new Prime Minister Tony Blair on Wednesday. The legislature will be disbanded by China and replaced by a China-appointed chamber on July 1.

"I hope to impress on Prime Minister Tony Blair and his ministers the importance of elected institutions, human rights and the rule of law to keeping Hong Kong a free and prosperous society," Lee said in a statement.
Also on Tuesday, a think tank closely associated with Tung launched a new index that will act as a barometer of Hong Kong's status as a free market economy after the sovereignty change.
China has promised the territory of 6.4 million that its freewheeling capitalist way of life will be kept intact for 50 years after the handover.
